projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Clarence C. Dye was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Lorraine Southward
sp.p: I have been transcribing. This is the first interview I have done. It is the first time I have done this. I know from my transcribing it begins like this: I am Lorraine Southward. I am at the home of CC Dye. It is November 24, 2007. I am about to talk to him about his military career. The first question I'm going to ask, CC -1 have known you many years. I have no idea what "CC" stands for. What is your full name as we would find it on your military records?

sp.speaker: Clarence C. Dye
sp.p: Clarence. Clarence C. Dye.

sp.speaker: Lorraine Southward
sp.p: Your address right now?

sp.speaker: Clarence C. Dye
sp.p: [Address redacted] - oh - you want the physical address? [redacted].

sp.speaker: Lorraine Southward
sp.p: Will you tell me where you were born? In Kansas. When? On November 1921. Now that's All Saints Day, and I'm the greatest saint of all! Right! I'll see that gets in the transcript. I'm not sure... well, never mind. Tell me when you joined the service.

sp.speaker: Clarence C. Dye
sp.p: In November 1939.

sp.speaker: Lorraine Southward
sp.p: Did you join because there was a war, or because you had made up your mind to be a military person?

sp.speaker: Clarence C. Dye
sp.p: Because I had made up my mind. There was no war on, except in Europe, at that time.

sp.speaker: Lorraine Southward
sp.p: Did you join up in your home town?

sp.speaker: Clarence C. Dye
sp.p: No. San Diego, California.

sp.speaker: Lorraine Southward
sp.p: Which branch did you join?

sp.speaker: Clarence C. Dye
sp.p: I joined the Marine Corps. U.S. Marine Corps.

sp.speaker: Lorraine Southward
sp.p: So you joined the "once a Marine, always a Marine" crowd! You said you had made a list of your activities. Let's start off, and you tell me about them. On November 1939, you were - what would you be?

sp.speaker: Clarence C. Dye
sp.p: Eighteen.

sp.speaker: Lorraine Southward
sp.p: So you waited until you were 18 years old - you were waiting to get in? Did you have family in the Marines that you were interested in it?

sp.speaker: Clarence C. Dye
sp.p: No. No. My father was in the Navy in World War I. I'm sure his belief influenced me, that - he was always saying - he worked for the railroad - but he was always saying, "If I had stayed in the Navy, I could have retired by now." I guess that impressed me. But any way - sideline. On the 1st of November I went out to the Navy base in San Diego to join. I got through the physical until I came to the dentist. They said, "You're rejected. You've got too many fillings. The Navy only allowed five fillings, and you have seven." So I went into the Marine Corps. They weren't interested in me biting the enemy. I joined up there. They signed me up on the 9th of November. On the 10th, I thought, "Boy! I've got the right place here." It was the Marine Corps Birthday, and we had turkey and all the trimmings. Each of us got what we called a bag of pogey-bait, which was candy.

sp.speaker: Lorraine Southward
sp.p: Pogey-bait?

sp.speaker: Clarence C. Dye
sp.p: That is a service term. - and a carton of cigarettes. Then on the 11th, it was a holiday again, so we got the same thing again. "Man," I thought, "I've got it going here!" On the 12th, though, the bottom fell out. We started basic training.

sp.speaker: Lorraine Southward
sp.p: Where? In San Diego?

sp.speaker: Clarence C. Dye
sp.p: San Diego Marine Base. A humorous incident there: we were issued equipment, and the Base Exchange, the DI - Drill Instructor was standing by the tobacco counter - and I marched up and said - because we were going to be eight weeks, no liberty, not out of the area at all - so I said, "Give me a carton of Luckies Cigarettes." And the DI says, "You don't make enough money, Boot, to buy tailor made cigarettes. Give him a carton of Bull Durham." So that's where we started from. Basic training - we lived in tents, two people to a tent. In eight days I wore the soles out of my shoes, even though they had been double-soled, on the parade ground learning to march. The training went well. You see in the movies today the DI hollering a lot. No hollering there. Very controlled, very firm. As an example, in the boot camp we did all our own laundry every night. We had white underwear. You couldn't have any civilian clothes, underwear or anything else. Strictly white. The wash rack was a long water trough with a scrub table. You scrubbed it. When you got through scrubbing, the DI would come back and you held them up so he could see against the sun. If there was any stain in them, he'd grab them out of your hand and grind them into the sand. He'd say, "Do'em again, Boot." That was the wash procedure - every day. Then, the other disciplinary measures - in the tent, there were no radios, and if somebody started singing back there, the DI would come by and find out who it was. He'd say, "We want you to appreciate this, too. So put this bucket over your head and go up and down the company street and sing as loud as you can, because you want you to hear it, and we want to hear it, too."

sp.speaker: Lorraine Southward
sp.p: How many people sang?

sp.speaker: Clarence C. Dye
sp.p: Not many! [laughs] Another thing was - for different infractions, you went to the beach with - we lived in the sand - but you went down to the water. You got two buckets of sand and ran back with them. He'd say - after about four buckets, "Oh. You've gotta take that back to the beach." So the boot would pick up the sand with his hands and take it back to the beach. The third serious punishment for an offense was a belt line. All the boots lined up on either side of the walk, and the individual took off his shirt, and he walked slowly down through there. We had leather belts then. You whacked him.

sp.speaker: Lorraine Southward
sp.p: You had to walk?

sp.speaker: Clarence C. Dye
sp.p: Oh, yes. You had to walk. The DI on each side would walk along. There were two DIs - a sergeant and a corporal. They would walk along either side. If somebody felt chick and didn't whack hard enough. "Okay, Boot. You go back. You get in the belt line." So that was the punishment. Everybody stayed in the line.

sp.speaker: Lorraine Southward
sp.p: What would you have to do to warrant the whacking in the line?

sp.speaker: Clarence C. Dye
sp.p: Miss formation. Be late for it. Be smoking when you weren't supposed to be. Be talking when you weren't supposed to be. Not being in proper clean uniform.

sp.speaker: Lorraine Southward
sp.p: I guess I would have done a lot of singing and tried to avoid the whacking! [laughs]

sp.speaker: Clarence C. Dye
sp.p: So that was that - for eight weeks. After that we could go ashore, leave the base on liberty. I was assigned to the 10th Marines, which was stationed there at the base, to an artillery outfit. The only mechanized weapon that we had was what they called the "Marmon Herrington." It was a tracked vehicle, kind of like a motor scooter today. One interesting thing: when we went to the rifle range there was only one truck there. It was an old hard-tired Liberty truck from World War I. The sergeant in charge had been in the German Army. He didn't speak English. And he couldn't write. It wasn't until he retired that they found this out. He had a notebook. When they told him what was to be done on maintenance or that, he drew a picture. He had notebooks and notebooks full of pictures. On joined the 10th Marines, I was selected for what they called "Sea School." There, you were learning what it was to be in the Navy, because we were going to be posted aboard ship as a Marine Guards detachment. So I went to Sea School. That's where I got my dress blues - that you see the Marines in now.

sp.speaker: Lorraine Southward
sp.p: That's sea school as in S-E-A - the ocean?

sp.speaker: Clarence C. Dye
sp.p: Yes. We completed that, and I was assigned to the USS Saratoga, which was then at Bremerton, Washington. Transporting us up to Washington - Bremerton - we rode the USS New Mexico - the battleship. It took us eight days to get there. We joined the Saratoga, and then after the yard period we came back to Long Beach. They had put a new gadget on this ship. As a Marine detachment, we had people who were captains' orderlies, the commanders' orderly, and gun strikers, watch people - so that we got all the information from the orderlies there about what was going on. Well, when you come from a yard period, you go 30 knots - as fast as you can - to test it out. The captain was relying on this new gadget - which happened to be a radar - and when we got to Long Beach, the radar officer says, "Sir, the radar hasn't been working since we left San Francisco." So we were plowing through all the shipping lanes, at night, at 30 knots! But we missed everything. One other thing - we were travelling blackout. They knew something was in the wind, but everywhere we went at night, we had no lights showing anywhere. That was in 1940. We were at Long Beach. We were there until November '40 and then they moved the entire fleet to Hawaii. I saw the last of the great fleets, where they had all the destroyers in the Pacific fleet in a line, then came the cruisers, then came the battleships, then came the carriers. That was the final of that type of operation.

sp.speaker: Lorraine Southward
sp.p: They went from the U. S. over to Hawaii in this kind of formation?

sp.speaker: Clarence C. Dye
sp.p: No. That happened - they moved all the ships over to Lahaina Roads, and we anchored there. Then from there we went to Pearl Harbor. That distance is when they formed that formation. After that, the Navy formed Task Force type things. We were there - 1940 - and then came back to the States to go in the yard the next year. ImadePFC. I made it ahead of time. They had a compulsory examination. I wasn't too popular, because I beat out a lot of guys who had been on there for a long time. I was just out of boot camp, so I knew what was going on. I was assigned as a gun striker, which was the maintenance of a 5-inch 25- caliber gun. We had two of them on the starboard side and the port side. I was on the port side, gun number 2. Then, that went on. I'll never forget - we went back to San Diego to do a yard period, because a bunch of ships were going into the yard. We were in San Diego, and December 7th, 1941, I was just going on corporal of the guard - I was on promotion list for corporal - and we had this metal locker that you unlocked - you got the revolvers out, pistols that the guards took, and you issued each one. While doing this, the announcement came over the PA system that the Japanese had just hit Pearl Harbor. So immediately the action started. We didn't have any planes on, so they started loading the aircraft. We took off the next day for a Hawaii.

sp.speaker: Lorraine Southward
sp.p: You are still on the Saratoga!

sp.speaker: Clarence C. Dye
sp.p: Still on the Saratoga - yes. We took off for Hawaii. It took six days to get there. We got there and of course things were in quite a turmoil. The next operation - let's see. We took off - Wake Island was under siege. Am I saying what you want?

sp.speaker: Lorraine Southward
sp.p: Absolutely.

sp.speaker: Clarence C. Dye
sp.p: We took off for Wake Island to try to save that, but we got halfway there and they called us back. We went back. They decided to abandon Wake Island. Then, of course, we went out on maneuvers all the time. It was interesting - we took on a new admiral - Fletcher. He had been a cruiser admiral. We went out on a shakedown cruise, so the captain could tell him how a carrier worked and what was the capability. Well, the first thing he said was - the flight deck - which was a huge thing - had just been stained ocean blue - and he said, "Why aren't you holy-stoning the deck?"

sp.speaker: Lorraine Southward
sp.p: Holy-stoning?

sp.speaker: Clarence C. Dye
sp.p: They had these blocks of stone and they went up and down and up and down on a board until it was smooth and white. Well, that would have been a tremendous job. They finally convinced him what it was supposed to be. We were committed to go in support of the Battle of Midway, but we didn't make it in time. Wound up then that we were the only carrier left because the other two - the Lexington and the other one we had - got hit at Midway. And the U.S. had only one carrier - that was us.

sp.speaker: Lorraine Southward
sp.p: During all this, while these things are happening, as a very young person on board, how much of what is going on all around you - around the world - for instance while you were in San Diego you heard that Pearl Harbor was hit - what do the boys - and you are boys at this point - what do you know about what is going on. Is there a lot of hearsay around the deck or do officers tell you the news?

sp.speaker: Clarence C. Dye
sp.p: We got our news from the orderlies. There were no briefings or any other information at that time.

sp.speaker: Lorraine Southward
sp.p: It is something that I have always been curious about, because you had to have wondered what was going on. Where were you going next, or whatever.

sp.speaker: Clarence C. Dye
sp.p: Yes. They pulled us back from Midway to Hawaii. Then we were committed to go to Guadalcanal. This is in'42. And I'll never forget - it was pitch black on the morning the attack was to take place. We were at gun stations, and the planes took off. The first plane to take off was what we called an SBD - it had 1,000 pound bomb on it. There were no catapults at that time. They just back them up on the flight deck, gave the engine all the RPMS they could, and rumbled down the deck. They would shake - and take off. This guy took off and he went straight in the water. That was our first offensive action - large-scale offensive action in the Pacific. He just went down. Never heard a word about who it was or anything. We completed that operation and were on the way back. Still dark, night, no moon. The cruiser San Francisco was on our port beam. I was on duty. It used a 36-inch spotlight and flashed "Torpedoes on the way" in Morse code. Well, two were on the way. One missed us and the other hit us. There were six crewmen in the engine room had perished. But they didn't open the engine room until they got back to Hawaii in dry dock, where they could get us patched up. While there, they had a submarine scare, [laughs] - I was on the port battery, as I said, and the gunnery officer - all we could see was dry land - the instructions were to search the surface for the submarines.

sp.speaker: Lorraine Southward
sp.p: And all you could see was dry land?

sp.speaker: Clarence C. Dye
sp.p: Yes. So we had the crews in the saddles, as they said - each gun had a pointer that pointed the gun (vertical) on the other side the traverse that covered the horizontal movement. The gunnery officer came by and says, "Why aren't you searching - like the order said?" I said, "All we can see is dry land. The crew is in position and ready." I got put on report. Well, we went to Captain's Mast, and they gave me some extra duty. But I'll never forget that. Stupid order. But Commander Pride upheld the gunnery officer and his discipline.

sp.speaker: Lorraine Southward
sp.p: You say the commander's name was Pride?

sp.speaker: Clarence C. Dye
sp.p: Yes. Anyway, I got over that. During the incident when we got hit, a Navy lieutenant came busting out of the hatch, and the light was shining and he was panicky. He said, "Commence firing! Commence firing!" Couldn't see anything. He was screaming. We had a warrant officer aboard, and he was on the battery with us, so we wrestled the guy to the deck. Warrant Officer Bickle sat on him, while he was screaming. Bickle had headphones on, and he talked to Sky Forward - the control officer way up there - and said, "We got one of your guys here that you might want to come down and get." Never saw that officer after that.

sp.speaker: Lorraine Southward
sp.p: That warrant officer was a Marine? And the guy who came out screaming was Navy?

sp.speaker: Clarence C. Dye
sp.p: Yes. The next day - we were dead in the water - the next day they mustered us on deck. The cruiser Minneapolis got in front of us. They fired a line overhead and hauled a 6-inch hawser over and connected it to us. The cruiser played out the line. That line went from 6 inches to 2 inches under the stress. The object was to get us going so we could get enough wind over the flight deck - which had to be at least 15 knots - to launch the planes. So here is the cruiser towing us and they launched all the planes. Then a sea tug that was in the area took us into Pearl Harbor to be patched up.

sp.speaker: Lorraine Southward
sp.p: So you were towed back to Pearl Harbor? Was the engine room still sealed? And the dead men in it?

sp.speaker: Clarence C. Dye
sp.p: Yes. Oh, yes. During this cruise, when we were out there, we went to Espirito Santos in the Suva Islands. Another quirk: a freighter came in with fresh meat. This was one of two incidents. They said, "Send a crew to unload the meat." The admiral in charge said, "I'm not having my sailors unload a ship. That's your job." So the meat spoiled.

sp.speaker: Lorraine Southward
sp.p: The meat spoiled!!??

sp.speaker: Clarence C. Dye
sp.p: Yes. There was about 8 or 10 tons. So that was an interesting thing. At the time I was promoted to gunnery sergeant, and I was in charge of the batteries. I went to Chiefs' Quarters. That was a privilege when you got that. Until this time we had lived in the hammocks. I preferred the hammocks because when the ship rolled you rolled right with it. There were about 20 of us in this compartment - all in the hammocks. We were right by the main elevator that they used to raise and lower planes from the hanger deck. We were lucky we could get a breeze through there. Otherwise - no ventilation. The hammock incident! had a false tooth plate in the front of my mouth. I had a peg tooth and they pulled it and made me a plate. I woke up in the middle of the night and my mouth felt cold. I said, "Oh, some S.O.B. has stolen my plate. Reached in my mouth and pulled it out!" So I got up and I was roaming around there - and I found it underneath my mattress in my hammock! So that was a kind of an interesting thing. But at Chiefs' Quarters, when I moved, I got a bunk. I was eight decks down. There were the fuel tanks, and a Chief Petty Officer and myself were in this. One night I woke up - I had a little Baby Ben clock. Those were in great demand there because my duties were 12 to 4 watch in the morning and at night. I did that all the time there. So the clock was essential, because when every morning you had general quarters before daylight and we went on complete lockdown. That's when attacks usually came. So I reached back and felt this hand behind my head. And I said, "Oh - you sunnuvabitch, you are trying to steal my clock!" Turned out it was my hand.

sp.speaker: Lorraine Southward
sp.p: Your own hand?

sp.speaker: Clarence C. Dye
sp.p: It was asleep, [laughs]

sp.speaker: Lorraine Southward
sp.p: Did your cabin mate hear you do that?

sp.speaker: Clarence C. Dye
sp.p: I don't know. He never said anything. But that is a kind of humorous incident. Another humorous incident was that at Chiefs' Quarters they have their own mess hall. They could go there for breakfast and order anything they wanted - bacon and eggs, hotcakes, waffles - whatever. These old chiefs - every Saturday morning they served beans and prunes and cornbread. That was the menu for breakfast. These old chiefs would bitch because - why can't we get any beans and cornbread? All we have is bacon and eggs. Then, after I got used to them, I wanted to know why we couldn't have more beans and cornbread! Because it was good. In December of '43 they brought the ship back to San Francisco and I was transferred off and went to Camp Elliot. I was placed in a replacement battalion training troops to go back over again. In May, I went back overseas again.

sp.speaker: Lorraine Southward
sp.p: Where was Camp Elliot?

sp.speaker: Clarence C. Dye
sp.p: San Diego. I went back overseas. I joined the 1st Marine Division. 4th Battalion, Marines - which was the medium artillery support for the division. It was interesting. Three battalions had pack howitzers - 75 caliber - that you could take apart. They were made to take apart and put on mules in the old days. That was our artillery for three battalions. We were the fourth battalion, which was general support. We had towed howitzers. Today they have 8 inch and all that. The fire power was limited. The heavy artillery was 155mm guns - they called them Long Toms - but that was Corps that would be assigned to us. I was assigned, as I said, the 4th Battalion, 11th Marines, Headquarters Battery. The Division had just come back from Australia where they had been regrouped after they took them off Guadalcanal. We were there, and we trained for our next operation, which was Peleliu on the Pulau Islands. We didn't know where we were going, but we were trained for that. A side note: Grapefruit juice was what we had a lot of. At that time, we called it "battery acid." When you drank it, it would tear your head off- so sour! Today - oh, it is delicious, but not then. But that was all you had - canned. No fresh stuff. We trained for the operation in the Pulau Islands. When we got there - Peleliu was coral, and the Navy guns could fire into it. But the coral was soft. The round would go in and explode, and you could see just a big cavern in there. It would penetrate so deep but it couldn't blow it out. When we landed with the artillery, the infantry was supposed to be halfway across the island by noon - we got there at 11 o'clock. When I hit the beach, here is this Marine half in the water, half out, with a 60 mortar. I said, "Where are the front lines?" He said, "This is it!" So there we were, all stacked up there. The howitzers were transported by Army ducks, which are amphibious trucks. We had no transportation except the ducks until later. Our water supply - we were limited to two canteens a day - period. For everything. If you ran out - that was it. The water came in, in 55-gallon drums that they dropped over the sides from LSTs and let float in. That's how we got our water. Some of the drums had been used - had fuel oil and gasoline in them - but the water tasted good! I'll never forget. They said, "Don't pick up any casualties." Of course, grave registration was to do that. If you pick them up and bury them, then they can't find them. Well, grave registration was way behind. I'll never forget - on the barbed wire on the beach some poor soul hung there for a week until they could get to him. We had one man killed in that.

sp.speaker: Lorraine Southward
sp.p: You were under orders not to do anything for that person?

sp.speaker: Clarence C. Dye
sp.p: That's correct. Because they were dead, and if you buried them, they couldn't find them. After the operation we went back to Pavuvu in the Russell Islands, where we had come from, to restage for the next operation. I was promoted to Sergeant Major at the time. We were training for Okinawa. We got there - and I'll never forget that day. It happened to be Easter Sunday, April Fool's Day, and our landing day.

sp.speaker: Lorraine Southward
sp.p: Well, that's some combination.

sp.speaker: Clarence C. Dye
sp.p: Yes. We landed on Blue Two Beach. The infantry had ladders - aluminum ladder - about 20 feet long - to scale the sea wall. Now, the battleships had tried to knock down the wall, but they had these ladders to climb up in order to get on the beach. We had an easier beach. When we got ashore, for the CP - Command Post - they had caves back in there - Oh, maybe 10 to 15 feet back with covers. So I broke open one of those and there were hundreds of pots in there. The remains of people. There was one body there - in a wooden box. We moved him out. He was sitting up in this box, with his hat on.

sp.speaker: Lorraine Southward
sp.p: An Okinawan?

sp.speaker: Clarence C. Dye
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Lorraine Southward
sp.p: Were the remains in the pots ashes?

sp.speaker: Clarence C. Dye
sp.p: Yes. Ancestors from way, way back.

sp.speaker: Lorraine Southward
sp.p: Had they been cremated?

sp.speaker: Clarence C. Dye
sp.p: No. We wanted to use the caves for protection in case of artillery attack. When we got situated a little bit, I noticed a huge pile of logs about 2 feet long and with three handles sticking above. And baskets - oriental baskets. Have you seen those? For carrying? I'll get one to show to you. [leaves to get basket from garage] Anyway that is what the Japanese used for them to tamp the dirt when they built the airport. I mean, they made hundreds of these and the Orientals had these baskets that they used as wheel barrows. They had maybe 600 laborers there and... this was their wheel barrow [shows a basket about 6 inches deep at center, maybe 2 feet diameter, in woven straw]. They use these today.

sp.speaker: Lorraine Southward
sp.p: How were these connected to the logs?

sp.speaker: Clarence C. Dye
sp.p: No. They used the logs to tamp the coral. They used these baskets to carry crushed coral up to the airport runway they were building. You can imagine the tremendous amount of work.

sp.speaker: Lorraine Southward
sp.p: Borders on medieval construction.

sp.speaker: Clarence C. Dye
sp.p: The typhoon hit while we were there, and all the ships pulled anchor and had to move out to sea. We ran low on ammo and supplies for a while. But in August of '45 I was sent back to OCS at Camp LeJeune. The night I was to go, I went up and met the sergeant that had travelled with me before. He was in an antiaircraft outfit. He was sleeping in a cave and had a tarp over it. He said, "Get back under here!" Because flak from the anti aircraft guns would come crashing down. And we did have one that went into the sand right in front of us. I dug down over a foot and couldn't find it. It went deeper that that.

sp.speaker: Lorraine Southward
sp.p: There were a lot of ways to get injured in that war!

sp.speaker: Clarence C. Dye
sp.p: Yes. The reason for the delay was the Japanese came in and destroyed all the transports that were on the airfield. So we had to wait until they brought more in to take us out. They took us to Saipan. And there - at an Air Base -1 wanted to kill this air man who was in line to get food, he said, "Oh, do we have to have eggs and bacon again?" We hadn't seen a fresh egg in over a year. Cook said to me, "How many would you like?" He maybe had a dozen there, and I said, "I'll take them all!" [laughs] So I got to LeJeune and was in OCS when the war ended. I decided that at age 23, I was top of the enlisted rank, I had six years of service. I didn't want to spend 24 more years at the same level, doing the same thing. So I decided to get out and go to college. I went to the Library of Congress in Washington and looked up a college that had Forestry and would be about 750 miles from my parents. I didn't want to be too close! I found the University of Montana had a Forestry School, but it wasn't recognized by the association. Colorado A and M had a Forestry School. So that is where I went. I took ROTC, still continuing a military connection. I joined the Colorado National Guard and was commissioned in that... [end of side 1 of tape].

sp.speaker: Lorraine Southward
sp.p: They are both working again. We left off with you going to Colorado A and M in Forestry - you joined ROTC, and you got commissioned in the Colorado National Guard.

sp.speaker: Clarence C. Dye
sp.p: When I was discharged from the Marine Corps, they gave me 200 dollars pay and that was it. The Marine Corps, when they discharged you, you got 200 dollars pay and said, "Good-Bye." And my uniform - that's all I had to wear. I had to buy civilian clothes. Well, I started school in January of 46. Finished school in June of 49, and accepted a regular commission in the Army. I was posted from here to Fort Riley, Kansas. I was a 2nd Lieutenant in the Armor. When I went in to my bunk in there, I looked across at the other bunk, and whoever was there had eight pairs of shoes under his bunk. I had two pairs. I wondered what the hell I had gotten into! So it turned out that it was Casper from the University of Illinois. They Army had what they called the Ground General School. Newly commissioned ROTC students - nationwide - and the West Point class of '49 and brought them to Fort Riley for school from August until the middle of December. This was the best thing they ever did. It gave the officers a chance to meet other career officers that you might never have a chance to meet again. It was really interesting to meet these fellows. Of course, some of them felt they were extremely important. Others just went along. In December I was posted to Fort Knox for the Armor Basic Course. That lasted until June. In April, Career Management came by and issued assignment orders. They called me out. I like to fainted. I wondered, "What have I done wrong now?" The officer said, "You have had so much time overseas, you can get any place in the U.S. that you want to go to." So I chose Fort Lewis, Washington. This was 1950 - April. Then I thought, "I don't want to go to Washington. I want to go overseas. I want to go to Europe." So they changed my orders, and sent me to Europe. Well, of course, Korea broke out then. Because Armor officers weren't needed very much in Korea, I was sent to Europe. I was assigned to the 3rd Battalion, 6th Armored Cavalry, I Company. This time, somebody, somewhere, said, "We are going to eliminate the cavalry titles, which were "troop," "squadron," - we are going to have all the same. Except the artillery - they'll have batteries. So you will become a company in a battalion. Well, that didn't last long. I was assigned to the CONSTAB - Constabulary - which was the police force for Germany. Theirs wasn't up and running yet. I was stationed at Deggendorf, Germany, on the Austrian border. Got there in August of 1950. Then in November they moved the battalion to Regensburg, Germany. We were given - each company was given two boxcars., ship all your gear, bunks, lockers, and personal equipment, and wound up in Kelley Barracks, Regensburg, Germany, which had just been renovated. Things were getting tight then. In 1952 the CONSTAB was eliminated, police responsibility was turned over to the German police. They had Bundes Grenshutes, the Border Polizei, and ourselves. We were patrolling the border on vehicles. Each had a different path. The Russians were making a move, and the rivers were very low in June. Both World War I and World War II started when the rivers were low, could be forded, time the Russians were on extensive maneuvers. The officials were concerned, the Russians wouldn't stop coming. We went in what they called "TM Two," which was a training mission that had the regular patrols on the border with the Germans and right behind we had another patrol in case people had gotten through and we could pick them up. Our jeeps were wearing out fast, running up and down on patrol. In the winter the military tires were like ice skates on the roads. A brilliant decision was made by somebody way up the line in ASAREUR, one more accident on the border, you relieve the commander. Well, with those slick tires, and the patrols, and the ice - we went through - the border company - commanders! In fact, they had to relieve a commander on the border before the next one left. And he was relieved, too, because he was a commander.

sp.speaker: Lorraine Southward
sp.p: All this because of slick tires. You said - all the way up to - where?

sp.speaker: Clarence C. Dye
sp.p: USAREUR.

sp.speaker: Lorraine Southward
sp.p: Let me get this clear in my mind. You were there and you were fearful that the Russians would come across the river. So this is 1951, and we, back here, had no idea, I'm sure, that you were fearful that the Russians might attack.

sp.speaker: Clarence C. Dye
sp.p: Oh, very concerned. The Cold War was on. The Berlin Airlift had already gone through. The Berlin Wall was being built - so. It was interesting. At that time, the Army also - being a cavalry unit - we were to operate behind the lines. And the mission was always that - you find 'em and fix 'em - and we'll kill 'em. That means bringing up heavy tanks and so forth. But we couldn't cross the little bridges that we used to and it limited the roads that we could use. Let me go back. My first run-in was when I was at Fort Riley at the Ground General School. I was assigned, while the class was waiting to start, as the Personnel - Billeting Officer. As students reported in two would be assigned to living quarters. Well, I assigned a white officer to bunk with a colored officer. This officer turned out to be from Georgia. And he raised hell. I wouldn't change him. I said, "He is a fellow officer." This was before integration. Well, they changed it. The other colored officer came to the rescue and said, "Well, we would rather be together." So that's the way it went there. That solved that problem. The guy who complained - he and I became good friends later on. I think he forgot about that. That was my first run-in with discrimination. It was quite provoked. Regensburg was quite an old town. The bridge going across the river was built by Marcus Aurelius in the 11th century. We were out in the field and I was with I Company. The company commander came up and said, "Pack your gear. Put it on the jeep, everything! And go back to Battalion headquarters!" I wondered, what did I do wrong? Well, I found out that I was being assigned as Commander of H Company, which was a great plum. But nobody told me until I got back there. So I took that on. After six months, they wanted to change around, so they gave me Tank Company. The battalion has three recon companies and one tank company. So I got Tank Company, which had 17 medium tanks.

sp.speaker: Lorraine Southward
sp.p: What was your rank at this time?

sp.speaker: Clarence C. Dye
sp.p: Lieutenant. In August of '53, I got orders to rotate back to the States, the Armor Advanced Course. I was assigned to the 3rd Armored Division to wait for the school to start. We had 45 tanks in each company and you kept one of the best of each crew as tank commander for the next cycle of training. Well, I kept one black fellow, who was good. At that time, the rosters would come down with the name and rank and then "Negro" or "White." That always made me mad. So I had the 1st Sergeant cross out the race annotation. And we would assign them regardless. Well, wouldn't you know - the black tank commander got two black cadets in his crew, and one white. These two black privates - they weren't worth the powder to blow 'em to hell. He did everything. And I knew it. He'd give up, and finally came in and said, "Sir, would you please break up my crew." So I did. You know, those two privates when they were put in with a white crew really blossomed and became some of the best.

sp.speaker: Lorraine Southward
sp.p: Well, how do you reckon that happened?

sp.speaker: Clarence C. Dye
sp.p: When he had them all together they weren't worth a damn. But when we split them up, they became good troopers. The battalion commander was black. His name was Harrison. A real nice person and a good officer. He was from Mississippi. This is the second incident of discrimination that I learned about. He had six children. To go back to Mississippi, he had to travel from Kentucky to Mississippi at night. There were no motels between there that would take blacks. I always felt bad, because he had more on the ball than 90 percent of all the southerners along the way there. But I felt bad about that.

sp.speaker: Lorraine Southward
sp.p: Discrimination has been a black mark on this nation - other countries, too.

sp.speaker: Clarence C. Dye
sp.p: Yes. I went to the Advanced Course and completed that. In April they came out with orders where you were going in June. I was assigned to Bozeman, Montana - ROTC duty - at Montana State College at that time. It is now a university. But when I got the orders, I got calls that said, "Do you know where you are going?" I said, "Yes." "They just had three feet of snow in 24 hours!" When we got there, the officers that were there - one was from North Carolina, one was from Minnesota. The one from North Carolina says, "Well, I thought when the snow came they would shut things down. But you know what? They didn't even slow down! They just put on their skis and classes didn't even stop."

sp.speaker: Lorraine Southward
sp.p: In all these moves and changes, did you get leave? Did you have time off? Did you see anything in Germany?

sp.speaker: Clarence C. Dye
sp.p: When I was in Germany, I travelled. Other officers had kids. I travelled. I camped through Europe. They had excellent camping facilities there.

sp.speaker: Lorraine Southward
sp.p: Were you married at the time?

sp.speaker: Clarence C. Dye
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Lorraine Southward
sp.p: When did you get married?

sp.speaker: Clarence C. Dye
sp.p: In October, 1945.

sp.speaker: Lorraine Southward
sp.p: 1945. Just as the war ended. I think I remember a story that you met Rachel when she was an officer and you were not.

sp.speaker: Clarence C. Dye
sp.p: No. This was at Camp Elliott. I was going to leave out any family stuff.

sp.speaker: Lorraine Southward
sp.p: But that is part of the social history. It is interesting.

sp.speaker: Clarence C. Dye
sp.p: Oh, well. I was at Camp Elliott, and I was 1st Sergeant. I kept getting calls from what they called the Reception Center. I didn't know what a Reception Center was. But this lady would call and ask, "Is Private Joe Blow available? His parents are here and want to see him." What the Marine Corps had done - a smart thing - they had built this building where families could come and their Marine could be sent to meet them. There were no clubs, no recreation facilities on the post at all. I kept getting these calls. I said, "I'm going to find out what in hell this Reception Center is." So I went up there, took a couple of sergeants with me. And there were two Marine sergeants there. One was the one that was calling. So we got it straightened out. Don't call during duty hours! We're busy. Turned out to be Rachel, later my wife. So we went out for a cup of coffee some weeks later, and got started there. While I was overseas, she went to OCS and was posted in Washington as a lieutenant. She was the casualty officer for the Marine Corps. Her job was - when the ticker tapes came through with the casualties - then she would start the process to notify the people. She was reading it when her brother's name came through. She was granted leave right away and got home before the folks even knew what had happened. Her brother was a Marine officer - a pilot. That's the reason she joined. She was the second platoon of women Marines in World War II. She was the first woman from New Mexico to join the Marines. She was also part of the first five to be posted to California, Camp Elliott. Well, she was there, and in August when I got orders back - we had communicated - and I sent her a dozen roses. Well, that was a wrong thing to do, because that got started!! [laughs]

sp.speaker: Lorraine Southward
sp.p: Yes - the dozen roses! I remember.

sp.speaker: Clarence C. Dye
sp.p: I got out before she did. She got out the 6th of November. I got out the 1st of November. I took a meat cutter job at Safeway, and that's the reason I don't buy hamburger anymore! They've cleaned it up a lot since then but... Anyway, we left in November. When I said we had 200 dollars - she had 200 dollars and that's all we had - and our uniforms.

sp.speaker: Lorraine Southward
sp.p: So she was with you then when you were in college?

sp.speaker: Clarence C. Dye
sp.p: Oh, yes. She taught school. Went to school and got her Master's. She was on the G.I. Bill. Another caveat here: When she was in the Corps, they marched these gals in 2-inch pumps, in the sand. Later on, her legs broke down - the veins. She had to have three operations on her veins - on her legs. They were still bothering her. But she was on disability - 10%. But the Government says - since you are married and your husband is on the G.I. Bill, you can't draw disability, that's too much money for you. So you go on the straight G.I. Bill. She got her Master's degree, taught school, and that's the way we got through.

sp.speaker: Lorraine Southward
sp.p: Was she with you in Germany? She got to travel with you?

sp.speaker: Clarence C. Dye
sp.p: Yes. When we came back in August of 1953 - since you have introduced Rachel into this - we bought a 1952 MG We brought it back. We landed in New York, they gave us so little time that we were still in uniform. They were having a heat wave. It was 106 degrees, and we were in wools. They put us up in a hotel the services had requisitioned. No air-conditioning in that section. And Angela was just two. She didn't eat for a week. She had just fruit juice.

sp.speaker: Lorraine Southward
sp.p: Where was Angela born?

sp.speaker: Clarence C. Dye
sp.p: In Germany. Regensburg.

sp.speaker: Lorraine Southward
sp.p: You said that the other officers had kids. And you went camping.

sp.speaker: Clarence C. Dye
sp.p: After she was born, we had a little chair we put in behind the seat in the MG and she would ride there. We toured all through Europe.

sp.speaker: Lorraine Southward
sp.p: I think you two had a lot of fun.

sp.speaker: Clarence C. Dye
sp.p: Oh, yes. We did travel. To digress a bit, when I was in the training Battalion at Fort Knox, the 1st Sergeant I had was black. He had a problem with the troops while I was out on the field. Some trooper was having problems and abandoned a baby there. Rachel was home, and about 6 o'clock at night, here comes Sgt. Tungstall, black, with this white baby. He came up to Rachel at the back door, he banged on it, and said, "Here!" and thrust the baby into her arms and left. He didn't know what to do with it. Rachel didn't know. I was out in the field. The MPs had the wife. The husband was in the company. We got it all ironed out. Another incident was that I had a Lieutenant Principi that was assigned to the company. He was from Chicago. His folks came down from Chicago. They were all dressed in black, in a big black limousine. Her son's name was Rocko. She said, "Rocko didn't get good Italian food." She brought spaghetti. I mean, big spaghetti! And she said, "Do you have a room?" They didn't have anywhere to go, so Rachel took them in at the house. She was going to cook dinner that night for Rocko. Okay. She asked if we had a big pot. Oh, sure. Pulled out this Wearever pot. I mean, a BIG pot! Well, the mess sergeant brought a 15 gallon stock pot out. In fact, he brought two of them. Spaghetti in one and the meat sauce in the other one. We had real spaghetti for Rocko. We had all the officers in and the neighbors, too. We took his parents out on the range for orientation - and they were in their black clothes, coat, and tie, hot. And it was dusty! So we put them on the tank where we were running a course - hot and dusty - and they really got dusted down. But they said, "Will Rocko have time off?" and I said, "No. Bring the folks out, and they can ride." So that day, they rode the tanks and saw what Rocko was doing, too. They came out well dusted. In August 1954 we were posted to the ROTC detachment at Montana State University at Bozeman, Montana. In August 1957 we had orders to Europe. Rachel said, "I'm not leaving the U.S. until we own part of it." So we heard about some land out in Gallatin Canyon. We bought 10 acres. We were going to buy 20 acres, but the locals said, "You're crazy to pay 150 dollars an acre for that!" They said it was only worth 11 dollars an acre. So we said we would just go half crazy and buy 10 acres. Well, you know what has happened to land values! We went back to Europe. In August, we had a '56 Plymouth convertible. Rachel and I left Angela with Oma - Rachel's mother - and we drove all the way across Canada, with the top down, and Rachel bitched all the way about her hair, [laughs] There were no quarters where we were going. Rachel went back to Aberdeen, South Dakota, and I went to Germany. I was assigned to the 7th Army Training Center, Range Control, in Grafenwoehr, which was a big training area. Rachel came over later. When she saw the place we were going to live, she went up in smoke. There were 21 coal buckets in the hallway. We had seven stoves. They used these little charcoal briquettes. The stoves took a couple of briquettes at a time. Oh, boy. She didn't want to go, anyway. But it turned out to be one of the best assignments we had. From there we were sent back to the Command General Staff School at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas. From there, we were posted to Fort Lewis, Washington. We were there - and enjoyed it tremendously. Rachel taught school. I called Career Management to ask about our future - we were going to buy a boat - this was in June. The officer said, "I don't think you should. I'm going to have to send you back to Europe." He said to go back to Montana State and finish the Master's Degree, and then go to Europe. So in August we went back to Bozeman, finished the Master's Degree in January, and went back to Germany.

sp.speaker: Lorraine Southward
sp.p: And at this time you were an Army officer - and you were going to school on Army money?

sp.speaker: Clarence C. Dye
sp.p: Yes. Yes. What they call "boot-strap." I was a Lieutenant Colonel. I was promoted while in Graduate School there. We were sent to Europe and assigned to Heidelberg as Assistant G-I for Manpower. Then in 1967, I was assigned as a commander of a 1st Recon Squadron, 2nd Cav, on the border of Bayreuth in Germany. The post was the only one up on top of a hill - everybody called it The Rock. This was during what they called "Drawdown." Vietnam was going full strength. We were losing people like mad. We came home to the post - we were just leaving on a Friday night, and we had a 20-passenger bus. On came the bus and there was one poor little kid on it. That was Angela. She had to go to high school in Nuremberg, which was 60 miles away. She was the only teenager on the post. We said, "This is not going to fly." We took leave and went to Switzerland to find a private school. The little lady that we talked to at the one school said, "Don't send your daughter here." This lady was a U.S. type teaching English there. She recommended this school at Gustadt, Switzerland. So we went up there. It was a great girls school. Angela would study in the morning, ski in the afternoon, study at night. That went on for the year there. When we left there, I had orders straight to Vietnam. Took them back to Bozeman, left them there, and took off for Vietnam. There I was assigned as the Deputy Chief of 28 Staff for the 4th Corps, which was at Cantow, in the Delta. I was put out at first because I didn't get a squadron to command. But I am glad I didn't because I got to work with the Vietnamese. We had only Vietnamese troops except one helicopter battalion. I was there for a year. It was interesting. We got attacked four times. Shows you how it can work. Lots of canals there in the delta. The enemy could put a mortar in a little sampan, come up alongside, put the mortar on the beach, fire a couple of rounds, put it back on the sampan, and leave. That was kind of what we are faced with right now. I completed the tour there and was assigned to Washington, Army Materiel Command, right by National Airport. We had a wonderful time. Angela was in college at Montana State. She wanted to do this, and do that. We told her she could go, do anything she wanted, but she had to get a teaching certificate. Women still had limited opportunities: clerical, nursing, teaching. She got through, too. Graduated with a language and education degree. When Rachel and I were in Washington, we voted for six months. This was in 1970. We hung a piece of paper on the refrigerator. Should we retire? Get an Army post? Or stay here? We each voted separately, and in six months elected to retire. And that ended my career.

sp.speaker: Lorraine Southward
sp.p: Ended your military career. In Washington, D.C. Well, how did you get to New Mexico?

sp.speaker: Clarence C. Dye
sp.p: We went back to Bozeman. I retired in March and in April I started to work for Montana State University. Then they put me in as Personnel Director. I happened to see an ad in the paper for a Personnel Director at New Mexico State University. I called Rachel and said, "I saw this in the Wall Street Journal. Do you want to go to New Mexico?" Oh, she loved Santa Fe. She had taught there. And that's where she entered the service from. She said, "Sure." So I put my oar in the water and they hired me. We moved to Las Cruces.

sp.speaker: Lorraine Southward
sp.p: Well, Las Cruces is not Santa Fe. Did Rachel adjust to Las Cruces?

sp.speaker: Clarence C. Dye
sp.p: Yes. She liked it.

sp.speaker: Lorraine Southward
sp.p: She always seemed to be happy there. CC, I think we have covered it all. The only thing that - having prepared that was really a good idea - I'm not even going to ask you one of the questions...

sp.speaker: Clarence C. Dye
sp.p: Go ahead. Ask me anything.

sp.speaker: Lorraine Southward
sp.p: Overall, as you look back, what do you think being in the military did for you as a person? How did it affect your attitude toward life?

sp.speaker: Clarence C. Dye
sp.p: I really didn't have an attitude until I joined the service. And it did everything for me. The Marine Corps got me started. Rachel helped. I just had a bench made for her - to go by her grave - that honors her. "In Honor and Memory of Rachel Haire Dye. 1st Lieutenant USMSWR." And then down below it states, "She Made Me What I Am." And I signed my name. We worked as a team. We went where they assigned us and made the best of it. Every place we went was just like we were going to be there forever. What other questions?

sp.speaker: Lorraine Southward
sp.p: Today the world is a different kind of place. Some ugly things are happening. Do you have anything to say to people who might read this 50 years from now when things might be a whole lot different? Some sociologist or historian may find this transcript - do you have anything you want to say to somebody coming along 50 or 100 years from now? Anything you want to tell them about how to behave?

sp.speaker: Clarence C. Dye
sp.p: Anything I would have to say would be dated. They have to make up their own minds.

sp.speaker: Lorraine Southward
sp.p: With that, we will quit. And thank you very much.
